explanations.explanation: Close, friend, but the text says more. The LORD says, “Judah will be besieged, as well as Jerusalem.” So Judah isn't off watching from the porch. It's right in the middle of this too.
That's right, friend. The LORD says, “Judah will be besieged, as well as Jerusalem.” Nobody gets a seat on the sidelines here. Both of them are in the thick of it.
That's it, baker. The LORD says, “all who would heave it away will be severely injured.” Lift with your knees, they always say. Doesn't help when the thing you're lifting is a whole city.
Nobody's carrying this one off, friend. The LORD says everyone who would heave it away will be severely injured. The ones doing the heaving are the ones who end up hurting.

explanations.answer: They will break it in pieces
explanations.explanation: The text never says anyone breaks it, friend. The LORD says, “all who would heave it away will be severely injured.” So the ones heaving are the ones who get hurt, and breaking isn't part of it.

That one's flipped around, friend. The LORD says, “I will keep a watchful eye on the house of Judah, but I will strike with blindness all the horses of the nations.” So Judah gets the watchful eye, and the nations' horses get the blindness. Easy to swap when you read fast.

Right, baker. The LORD says, “I will keep a watchful eye on the house of Judah, but I will strike with blindness all the horses of the nations.” So the blindness goes to the nations' horses, and Judah gets the watchful eye. A panicked horse that can't see is going to make for a very long day for its rider.

explanations.answer: Because the LORD of Hosts is their God
explanations.explanation: That's the reason, baker. The leaders say, “The people of Jerusalem are my strength, for the LORD of Hosts is their God.” That little word “for” is where the reason starts.

explanations.answer: Because Jerusalem has the strongest walls
explanations.explanation: The text never says a word about walls, friend. The leaders say the people of Jerusalem are their strength “…for the LORD of Hosts is their God.” The reason is who their God is.

explanations.answer: Because the nations have all gone home
explanations.explanation: Not so, friend. Just before this, the LORD says “…all the nations of the earth gather against her…” The leaders' reason is that the LORD of Hosts is the God of Jerusalem's people.

explanations.answer: They will be consumed on the right and the left
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The LORD says the clans of Judah “…will consume all the peoples around them on the right and on the left…” So the peoples around them are consumed, on both sides. Judah is the firepot in that woodpile.

explanations.answer: They will put out the fire of Judah
explanations.explanation: Other way around, friend. The text says the clans of Judah “…will consume all the peoples around them…” Judah is like a firepot in a woodpile, and the peoples around them are the ones consumed.

explanations.answer: They will run to Judah for shelter
explanations.explanation: That's not what the text says, friend. It says Judah “…will consume all the peoples around them on the right and on the left…” The peoples around them are the ones consumed, and shelter isn't mentioned.

Yes, baker, that's what the text says. The LORD says He will make the clans of Judah like a firepot in a woodpile, like a flaming torch among the sheaves. Then He says they “…will consume all the peoples around them on the right and on the left, while the people of Jerusalem remain secure there.” So Judah's clans are the firepot, and Jerusalem's people are the ones who stay secure.
The text says the opposite, friend. While Judah's clans consume the peoples around them, “…the people of Jerusalem remain secure there.” Secure is the word the LORD uses.

explanations.answer: So King David's family and Jerusalem won't outshine Judah
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The LORD saves Judah's tents first “…so that the glory of the house of David and of the people of Jerusalem may not be greater than that of Judah.” Judah's tents come first, and that's the reason the LORD gives.

explanations.answer: So Judah can lead the march to Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention any march, friend. It gives the reason: “…so that the glory of the house of David and of the people of Jerusalem may not be greater than that of Judah.” So the LORD is looking out for Judah's share of the glory.

explanations.answer: So Judah can rebuild the walls of the city
explanations.explanation: Nothing about rebuilding walls here, friend. The reason the text gives is “…so that the glory of the house of David and of the people of Jerusalem may not be greater than that of Judah.” That's about the glory of David's house and Jerusalem's people not being greater than Judah's.

That's right, baker. The LORD says He will defend the people of Jerusalem “…so that the weakest among them will be like David…” David became king over Israel (2 Samuel 5:3). That's a big promise for the weakest.

The text says it plain, friend. The LORD will defend the people of Jerusalem “…so that the weakest among them will be like David…” David became king over Israel (2 Samuel 5:3). Even the weakest get to be like him.
That's the word, baker. The LORD says, “So on that day I will set out to destroy all the nations that come against Jerusalem.” He's the one who sets out. It's His own move.

Not this time, friend. The text says the LORD will “…set out to destroy all the nations that come against Jerusalem.” Bless is a warm, cozy word, like a fresh batch out of the oven. It's just not the one in this verse, and the verb here is destroy.

Forgive is a good word, friend, one I'd hang over my oven door. But the LORD says He will “…set out to destroy all the nations that come against Jerusalem.” The verb here is destroy, and forgive doesn't show up in the verse.

explanations.answer: A spirit of grace and prayer
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The LORD says, “…I will pour out on the house of David and on the people of Jerusalem a spirit of grace and prayer…” Grace and prayer. That's a gift poured out on them.
No sleeping here, friend. The LORD says He will pour out “…a spirit of grace and prayer…” That's what lands on the house of David and Jerusalem.

Not this time, friend. The cup in this chapter was a cup of drunkenness for the surrounding peoples (Zechariah 12:2). What He pours out on David's house and Jerusalem is “…a spirit of grace and prayer…”
That's the word, baker. The LORD says, “…they will look on Me, the One they have pierced. They will mourn for Him…” I think this one hurts. They'll look at Him and the grief will be real.
Not here, friend. The LORD says, “They will mourn for Him as one mourns for an only child…” I think this part is heavy, and the verse gives it room.
Hide isn't the word, friend. The LORD says, “…they will look on Me, the One they have pierced.” Then, “They will mourn for Him…” So the verse has them look and mourn.
That's right, baker. The text says, “They will mourn for Him as one mourns for an only child…” That's a deep kind of grief, and the verse says it just that way.

The text says it straight, friend. The LORD says, “They will mourn for Him as one mourns for an only child…” The ones mourning are the house of David and the people of Jerusalem. I think this picture is heavy.

That's the word, baker. The LORD says the fountain is opened “…to cleanse them from sin and impurity.” A fountain is for washing, and I know what a flour-covered apron needs. What this one washes away is sin and impurity.
Sickness is a fair guess, friend, since cleansing sounds like medicine. But the fountain is opened “…to cleanse them from sin and impurity.” Sickness isn't in that verse. Sin and impurity are.
Sorrow is an easy one to grab, friend, especially with all the mourning right before this. But the fountain is opened “…to cleanse them from sin and impurity.” The word in the verse is sin.
Other way around, friend. The LORD says, “…I will erase the names of the idols from the land, and they will no longer be remembered.” Not even a name tag left behind.
That's right, baker. The LORD says He will erase the names of the idols from the land, “…and they will no longer be remembered.” They get erased and forgotten.

explanations.answer: Spoken falsely in the name of the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says, baker. His father and mother say, “You shall not remain alive, because you have spoken falsely in the name of the LORD.” I'll say it once: this is a heavy part. The charge is about speaking falsely in the LORD's name.

explanations.answer: Turned away from working the land
explanations.explanation: That's not in the verse, friend. The parents say, “…because you have spoken falsely in the name of the LORD.” That's the charge. It's a heavy part, so I'll stick to what the text says.

explanations.answer: Stolen from the house of the LORD
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention stealing, friend. His parents say it's “…because you have spoken falsely in the name of the LORD.” It's a heavy part, so I'll leave it at what the verse says.
Yes, baker. On that day the prophet “…will not put on a hairy cloak in order to deceive.” So the cloak stays off. The verse says he's ashamed of his vision.
The text says the opposite, friend. On that day the prophet “…will not put on a hairy cloak in order to deceive.” The costume stays in the closet.

explanations.answer: Not a prophet but a servant who works the land
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. He says, “I am not a prophet; I work the land, for I was purchased as a servant in my youth.” That's how he describes himself, with no cloak and no big title. One short bio.

explanations.answer: Not a prophet but a priest in the temple
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say priest, friend. He says, “I am not a prophet; I work the land, for I was purchased as a servant in my youth.” Priest isn't in what he says, and neither is the temple.

explanations.answer: Not a prophet but a merchant from Tarshish
explanations.explanation: No merchant in this verse, friend. He says, “I am not a prophet; I work the land, for I was purchased as a servant in my youth.” Tarshish never comes up.

explanations.answer: He received them in the house of his friends
explanations.explanation: That's his answer, baker. He says, “These are the wounds I received in the house of my friends.” I think that's a rough place to get hurt. The text doesn't say more than that.

explanations.answer: He received them while working in the fields
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that, friend. He answers, “These are the wounds I received in the house of my friends.” The fields don't come up.

explanations.answer: He received them in a battle long ago
explanations.explanation: No battle in the verse, friend. He says, “These are the wounds I received in the house of my friends.” That's the whole answer.

That's the word, baker. The LORD of Hosts says, “Strike the Shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered…” Jesus quotes this line to His disciples (Matthew 26:31). It's a heavy moment, and the text says scattered.
Not this time, friend. The verse says, “Strike the Shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered…” The sheep scatter, and that's a heavy moment.
Counted isn't the word, friend. The verse says, “Strike the Shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered…” Scattered is what happens to the sheep. I think this one is heavy.

explanations.answer: Refine them like silver and test them like gold
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The LORD says, “This third I will bring through the fire; I will refine them like silver and test them like gold.” It's fire, but He's the one bringing them through it. And He's not done with them after that.

explanations.answer: Burn them away from the land for good
explanations.explanation: Not what the verse says, friend. The LORD says He will bring this third through the fire and “…refine them like silver and test them like gold.” After that, they call on His name and He answers.

explanations.answer: Punish them and then leave them behind
explanations.explanation: The text never says He leaves them, friend. He says, “I will refine them like silver and test them like gold.” Then, “They will call on My name, and I will answer them.” So this third gets refined and answered.
That's right, baker. The LORD says, “They will call on My name, and I will answer them.” They call, and He answers. It's that plain.

The text says the opposite, friend. The LORD says, “They will call on My name, and I will answer them.” So the calling comes first, and then the answer comes from Him. Saying False would leave out half of that line.

That's what He says, baker. The LORD says, “I will say, ‘They are My people,’ and they will say, ‘The LORD is our God.’…” Notice that both sides speak. He names them His, and they name Him their God. I think that's a family kind of line.
Debt is a clever guess, friend, like a bill stamped paid. But that's not what the LORD says. He says, “They are My people…” and they reply, “The LORD is our God.”
The text doesn't say that, friend. The LORD says, “They are My people…” and they say, “The LORD is our God.” Zion isn't part of that verse.
